name: Battle of San Jacinto

phases.title: The armies face each other across the grass
phases.text: Houston drew up the Texian line with the second regiment on the left, Burleson in the centre, the artillery and Millard's companies on the right and the cavalry on the extreme right. The Mexican troops lay behind breastworks in their camp.

phases.title: The cavalry go wide and the guns move up
phases.text: The Texian cavalry was sent to the Mexican far left, and the artillery advanced through the tall grass to within 200 yards of the breastworks.

phases.title: The Twin Sisters open the battle
phases.text: The Texian guns, within 200 yards of the Mexican breastworks, fired the Twin Sisters at 4:30 and began the battle.

phases.title: The Texians swarm over the breastworks
phases.text: After a single volley the Texians broke ranks and swarmed over the breastworks to fight hand to hand. The Mexican soldiers were taken by surprise, and Santa Anna and his officers shouted conflicting orders.

phases.title: The Texian infantry take the woodland and the breastwork
phases.text: The Texian infantry advanced without halt until they held the woodland and the Mexican breastwork. The right wing of Burleson's force and the left wing of Millard's took the breastwork.

phases.title: The Mexican troops abandon the camp and flee
phases.text: Within 18 minutes the Mexican soldiers abandoned their campsite and fled. Santa Anna escaped towards Vince's Bridge.

phases.title: Pursuit to Peggy Lake
phases.text: Many Mexican soldiers retreated through the marsh to Peggy Lake, where Texian riflemen stationed themselves on the banks and shot at anything that moved. The killing lasted for hours.

note: The accounts do not give compass directions or the exact positions of the Mexican troops, who are shown as one body behind their breastworks. The Mexican camp lay on a plain with woods on one side and marsh and lake on another; the plan puts the woods at the left and the marsh and lake at the top, and does not claim these were their true bearings. Vince's Bridge lay about 8 miles from the Texian camp, so only the direction Santa Anna took is drawn. The Texian riflemen on the lake banks are shown as a small part of the Texian infantry; the accounts do not say which regiment supplied them.
